items.title: ‘I Know God’s Power’: Dallas Jenkins Reacts Moments After Filming Last-Ever ‘The Chosen’ Scene
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: The end of an era.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

“The Chosen” creator Dallas Jenkins was filled with gratitude last Thursday night just moments after filming the final scene of his popular biblical series.

Jenkins, who exclusively invited CBN News on set in Texas to witness those last moments, expressed his profound gratitude for how the show is coming to an end.

“I feel awesome because there’s no more days hanging over my head, no more seasons hanging over my head, we’ve done the work that we set out to go,” he said. “God provided everything that we needed.”

The last scene, which featured the disciples on a boat, was memorable because the vessel used in filming was the same seen in the first season of the show. The scene offered a literal and figurative full-circle moment.

“God has met us here in the waters so often,” Jenkins said. “I have nothing but gratitude.”

Ultimately, Jenkins said the mission behind the show has never changed, even as the audience has swelled to over 100 million people.

“We haven’t changed,” he said. “We’re still trying to do the work for God. We’re still humbled, we’re still surrendered, we’re still grinding.”

As for how the seven-season journey changed Jenkins, he said it offered him insight into God’s character and relationship with mankind.

“I’ve been a believer as long as I can remember,” he said. “I know God’s power. … I don’t think I knew quite as much as I do now from doing this show how intimate of a God He is, how personal of a God he is.”

items.title: How Hunting for Deer Helped One Man Overcome His Wife’s Cancer Diagnosis
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Inspiring.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Though many years apart, James Hampton learned similar lessons about God, first through a cancer battle and later when he harvested a 150-inch buck on a hunting trip.

James and his twin brother Chad, now both pastors, grew up in a Christian home and were early followers of Jesus — and quick studies in the deer stand, too. As kids, hunting was a hobby that quickly blossomed into something more, and ultimately became the vehicle for their evangelistic mission today.

“During my wife’s cancer battle, God really spoke to both of us through that battle,” James said during a recent appearance on CBN’s “Faith in Culture” podcast, noting he and his wife were particularly drawn to James 1:2-3, where it’s written, “Dear brothers and sisters, when troubles of any kind come your way, consider it an opportunity for great joy. For you know that when your faith is tested, your endurance has a chance to grow” (NLT).

He continued, “That’s what God does through the waiting, through the trials, through the hard times, and definitely through the cancer battle that my wife went through. He really created perseverance in us, and it’s the same way in hunting.”

At first, that may seem like a peculiar connection — particularly to people who have never hunted.

But, as James said, “there’s a lot of waiting involved in hunting.” The same is true, at times, of waiting for God’s answers to prayer.

The preacher explained he put in more than 100 hours of waiting in the tree stand and, once the timing lined up just right, it was only a matter of seconds — 10, to be exact — before it was all over: he and Chad finally nabbed a 150-inch buck.

“It’s the same way on our hunt for God,” said James. “There’s so much waiting and patience and perseverance.”

As guys with a knack for hunting, they feel naturally at home using sportsman’s language to understand their faith. In fact, their organization, Huntin’ the Truth Ministries, was born out of that correlation.

King David’s writing in Psalm 14:2 has become an anchor for their ministry. In it, he wrote, “The Lord looks down from heaven on the entire human race; he looks to see if anyone is truly wise, if anyone seeks God” (NLT).

The Hampton twins, co-authors of the new devotional, “100 Days of Strength for Hunters,” interpret David’s writing through their passion for hunting. Strong’s Concordance defines “seek” as “investigate,” “enquire,” “study,” “practice,” and “follow.”

“God looks down from heaven on all of us, the sons of men, to see if there are any who understand or any who hunt for Him,” James said.

It was James’ wife’s fight against cancer that God used to bring that Psalm to James’ mind. He said, “[I was] hunting for my own plan for so long.” It wasn’t until he reached the end of himself, he said, that James found himself in the tree stand one night, where he started talking to God about his fears and frustration.

When he’s out hunting, James said, he always carries a small camo Bible in his backpack. He opened the Scriptures and God guided him to Psalm 14.

“It was that night God kind of slapped me across the face and made me realize … that He wanted me to hunt for Him like I hunt for deer,” James recalled. “He wants us all to hunt for Him, to search for Him, to seek for Him. … And I knew what He was talking about, because I knew how much of a diehard hunter I was and how much passion I had for hunting and how many hours I put in for hunting.”

He added, “God was telling me, ‘I want you to do the same thing: I want you to hunt for Me that hard. Seek Me that hard, with all your heart.'”

Listen to our full conversation in the “Faith in Culture” podcast episode above.

items.title: Is This News or Truth?
items.author: Lysa Terkeurst
items.summary: News and truth aren’t always one and the same. I learned this through a medical situation I faced a few years ago. It all started with words from my doctor that I never expected to hear. “Lysa, I’m so sorry. You have cancer.” I wish I could properly describe what happened in that moment. Everything&
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

News and truth aren’t always one and the same.

I learned this through a medical situation I faced a few years ago. It all started with words from my doctor that I never expected to hear.

“Lysa, I’m so sorry. You have cancer.”

I wish I could properly describe what happened in that moment. Everything around me got incredibly quiet and seemed to move very slowly. I could hear the doctor continuing to talk, but I couldn’t make out his words. I could feel words trying to form in my mouth, but there was no energy to actually speak. I knew I should probably cry, but no tears seemed available.

I am absolutely a woman who believes with all my heart that the presence of God is in the midst of my life. But in that moment, He felt distant and mysterious. I just felt stunned. And then I felt okay. And then I felt stunned again.

I wanted to hold it together. But then falling apart seemed quite reasonable.

It’s scary when doctors shock you with test results, and you don’t know what the future holds. I had come to the end of what I could do. I was forced to accept the harsh reality that there was nothing I could do to fix or change any of this.

In the days that followed my cancer news, God tenderly reminded me of an email my sweet friend Shaunti once sent me about another difficulty I was walking through. Her note said, “Lysa, this is news. This is not truth.”

Wow.

I’ve always thought of news and truth as one and the same. What the doctor gave me was news. Honest news, based on test results and medical facts.

But I have access to a truth that transcends news. The restoration that is impossible with human limitations is always possible for a limitless God. Truth is what factors God into the equation.

So, I found myself looking at the word impossible a little differently.

“Impossible,” in light of Shaunti’s note, could be completely different if I just stick an apostrophe between the first two letters. Then it becomes I’m-Possible. God is the Great I AM. Therefore, He was my possibility for hope and healing.

I’m-Possible is a much more comforting way to look at anything that feels quite impossible.

I suspect many of us have things in our life that feel impossible. Maybe you just got some bad news. News of an impossible financial situation. News of an impossible job situation. News of an impossible kid situation. News of an impossible friend situation. News of an impossible medical situation.

You may feel like you’re spiraling. You may feel like you want to try to take control to get to a different outcome. You may be wondering how God could let this happen. Trust me when I say I understand. Whatever news you just got or will get, I pray Shaunti’s advice helps you, too.

That is news.

And this is God’s Truth:

I AM THE WAY AND THE TRUTH AND THE LIFE.
“I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

I AM FOREVER FAITHFUL.
“He is the Maker of heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them — he remains faithful forever” (Psalm 146:6, NIV).

I AM WITH YOU.
“So do not fear, for I am with you; do not be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you and help you; I will uphold you with my righteous right hand” (Isaiah 41:10, NIV).

I AM HOLDING YOU.
“Yet I am always with you; you hold me by my right hand” (Psalm 73:23, NIV).

I AM YOUR HIDING PLACE.
“You are my hiding place; you will protect me from trouble and surround me with songs of deliverance” (Psalm 32:7, NIV).

One of the greatest comforts to me through all I went through was knowing that somehow, God would use it for good. And that God would be my possible in the midst of what can sometimes feel so impossible.

Of course, I still have those less spiritually secure moments when I feel like I’m going to lose my mind. And cry. And doubt that God will bring about good from what feels impossibly hard. But He will. He didn’t answer my prayers exactly as I hoped with my diagnosis and yes, I had to go through a battle, but today I’m cancer free.

I don’t know what the future holds but what I do know is how thankful I am for the Great I AM. The One who will absolutely “Guide me in [His] truth and teach me” (Psalm 25:5a, NIV).

I love you, sweet friend. And I’m praying for you today. Praying that every time the word impossible creeps up and starts to steal your hope, you will see the words I’m-Possible and hold on to Him.

ABOUT LYSA TERKEURST: Lysa TerKeurst is president and chief visionary officer of Proverbs 31 Ministries and the author of seven New York Times bestsellers, including I Want to Trust You, But I Don’t, Good Boundaries and Goodbyes, Forgiving What You Can’t Forget, and It’s Not Supposed to Be This Way. Her latest book is Making Peace With What I Can’t Control. She enjoys life with her husband, Chaz, and her kids and grandkids. Connect with her at www.LysaTerKeurst.com or on social media @LysaTerKeurst.

items.title: Sunday, October 4, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, just before his passion and death, Jesus tells this striking story of the landowner who planted a vineyard.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Isaiah 5:1-7

Let me sing for my beloved
my love-song concerning his vineyard:
My beloved had a vineyard
    on a very fertile hill.
He dug it and cleared it of stones,
    and planted it with choice vines;
he built a watchtower in the midst of it,
    and hewed out a wine vat in it;
he expected it to yield grapes,
    but it yielded wild grapes.
And now, inhabitants of Jerusalem
    and people of Judah,
judge between me
    and my vineyard.
What more was there to do for my vineyard
    that I have not done in it?
When I expected it to yield grapes,
    why did it yield wild grapes?
And now I will tell you
    what I will do to my vineyard.
I will remove its hedge,
    and it shall be devoured;
I will break down its wall,
    and it shall be trampled down.
I will make it a waste;
    it shall not be pruned or hoed,
    and it shall be overgrown with briers and thorns;
I will also command the clouds
    that they rain no rain upon it.
For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts
    is the house of Israel,
and the people of Judah
    are his pleasant planting;
he expected justice,
    but saw bloodshed;
righteousness,
    but heard a cry!

Psalm
Psalm 80:9, 12, 13-14, 15-16, 19-20

You cleared the ground for it;
    it took deep root and filled the land.
Why then have you broken down its walls,
    so that all who pass along the way pluck its fruit?
The boar from the forest ravages it,
    and all that move in the field feed on it.
Turn again, O God of hosts;
    look down from heaven, and see;
have regard for this vine,
the stock that your right hand planted.
They have burned it with fire, they have cut it down;
    may they perish at the rebuke of your countenance.
Restore us, O Lord God of hosts;
    let your face shine, that we may be saved.

Second Reading
Philippians 4:6-9

Do not worry about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

Finally, beloved, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is pleasing, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence and if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things. Keep on doing the things that you have learned and received and heard and seen in me, and the God of peace will be with you.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 21:33-43

“Listen to another parable. There was a landowner who planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a wine press in it, and built a watchtower. Then he leased it to tenants and went to another country. When the harvest time had come, he sent his slaves to the tenants to collect his produce. But the tenants seized his slaves and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. Again he sent other slaves, more than the first; and they treated them in the same way. Finally he sent his son to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir; come, let us kill him and get his inheritance.’ So they seized him, threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him. Now when the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?” They said to him, “He will put those wretches to a miserable death, and lease the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the produce at the harvest time.”

Jesus said to them, “Have you never read in the scriptures:
‘The stone that the builders rejected
    has become the cornerstone;
this was the Lord’s doing,
    and it is amazing in our eyes’?

Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people that produces the fruits of the kingdom.

Reflection

Friends, just before his passion and death, Jesus tells this striking story of the landowner who planted a vineyard. The fertile vineyard stands for Israel, his chosen people. But it could be broadened out to include the world. What do we learn from this beautiful image? That God has made for his people a place where they can find rest, enjoyment, and good work.

We—Israel, the Church, the world—are not the owners of this vineyard; we are tenants. One of the most fundamental spiritual mistakes we can make is to think that we own the world. We are tenants, entrusted with the responsibility of caring for it, but everything that we have and are is on loan. Our lives are not about us.

Christ is God’s judgment. We are all under his judgment. In the measure that we reject him or refuse to listen to him, we place our tenancy in jeopardy. And so the great question that arises from this reading: How am I using the gifts that God gave me for God’s purposes? My money? My time? My talents? My creativity? My relationships? All is for God, and thus all is under God’s judgment.

items.title: St. Francis and Sister Death
items.author: Dr. Hannah Barrett
items.summary:
Dr. Hannah Barrett

What does Francis’s death teach us about conforming ourselves to God’s will in the face of death?
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Hannah Barrett

This year, the Church celebrates the 800th anniversary of the death of St. Francis of Assisi. While Pope Leo XIV proclaimed the entire year a jubilee in Francis’s honor, we approach a high point of celebration with his feast day on October 4. In his humility, St. Francis may appreciate that the Twenty-seventh Sunday in Ordinary Time supersedes the liturgical celebration of his feast day on the 800-year mark, with the Church’s weekly celebration of Christ’s resurrection superseding the saint’s death. But Franciscans around the world will still commemorate the death of their spiritual father, beginning the evening of October 3 (the anniversary of his death) with a memorial service called the Transitus—the “passing over” of Francis from this life to the next. This time in the Jubilee year is an apt moment to pause and note the remarkable death of this even more remarkable saint.

The early biographer Thomas of Celano reports that at the hour of his death, Francis encouraged his brothers to read the Gospel story of Christ’s washing the feet of his disciples, to recite Psalm 142 (Francis’s favorite), and to sing “The Canticle of the Creatures,” which Francis had composed in pieces at the end of his life. The service of the Transitus involves these elements and recollections from Francis’s life as well as his final words, reported in the biography composed by St. Bonaventure: “I have done what was mine to do; may Christ teach you what is yours.” But St. Francis was still in the midst of his final task: that of dying well.

We see this most poignantly with the addition on his deathbed of a final verse to his “Canticle of Creatures.” After praising God through Brother Sun and Sister Moon, Brother Wind and Sister Water, Brother Fire and Sister Mother Earth, and through peacemaking, Francis turns to face death:

Praised be You, my Lord, through our Sister Bodily Death,
from whom no one living can escape. 
Woe to those who die in mortal sin. 
Blessed are those whom death will find in Your most holy will, 
for the second death shall do them no harm.

Because Francis praises God through “our Sister Bodily Death,” death is sometimes interpreted, for Francis, as another part of God’s family of creatures. But the Catechism of the Catholic Church teaches that death, while natural, is a consequence of sin (CCC 1008). It is the undoing of life in two respects: a separation of body from soul and bodily decay (CCC 997). It entails separation from loved ones. There is no need to mince words about the tragic nature of death, even for those who long to be with the Lord and hope for a Christian death (CCC 1010). Death is repugnant to the creation through which Francis praises God. Why, then, in the “Canticle” does Francis approach death—“from whom no one living can escape”—as a sister, a figure typically seen as comforting and caretaking? Francis’s manner of dying, as well as the “Canticle” itself, may provide insight. 

Francis’s sequela Christi—“following of Christ”—included the stigmata. This participation in the physical wounds of Christ’s passion manifests an astounding conformation to Christ in his suffering and love. But death was Francis’s final step in the sequela Christi of this life. While dying, Francis asked to be placed naked on the earthen floor to draw nearer to Christ in his passion. The dynamic of Francis’s ardent desire to conform to Christ here reaches its depth: from wealth to poverty, from health to a broken body, and, finally, from life to death. Each of us will follow Christ into death, but will we imitate him in death, as Francis did, by embracing Christ in his humiliation? While the stigmata is a gift given to few saints, participation in death as a sequela Christi is a gift offered to all souls. It is God’s final offering in this life to conform ourselves to Christ. For Francis it becomes a comfort that death—sisterly death—offers the possibility to cling more closely to Christ in this final act of life.

Francis knows that his final act of conformation to Christ will be sisterly if he is found in God’s “most holy will”—as Christ obeyed the Father’s will in Gethsemane. What does Francis’s death teach us about conforming ourselves to God’s will in the face of death? In singing the “Canticle,” Francis provides another template for a holy death: praise of God. Eight times throughout the “Canticle,” Francis proclaims, “Praise be You, my Lord.” He first praises God through six elements of creation, calling to mind the six days of creation. This prepares his seventh proclamation, recalling the peace and rest of the seventh day: 

Praised be you, My Lord, through those who give pardon for Your love, 
and bear infirmity and tribulation. 
Blessed are those who endure in peace 
for by You, Most High, shall they be crowned.

Having asked to lie naked on the earth, touching the dust to which he would return, Francis offered forgiveness and blessing to his brothers. Pope Leo opened the Jubilee Year of Francis with a prayer that we, like Francis, might become “unarmed and disarming witnesses to peace.” This is the witness of Francis, even in his final hour. Unarmed in the face of death and disarming his companions with a peace that is ushered in through praise of God, he offers a praise that bears ills and wrongs with forgiveness. 

This leads St. Francis to his eighth proclamation of praise: “Praise be you, My Lord, through our Sister Bodily Death.” After six praises through creation and a seventh praise through peacemaking that brings rest, Francis’s praise of God through death recalls the Church’s celebration of the eighth day. This refers to the new creation initiated by Christ’s resurrection and bears the hope of our own. Praising God through Sister Death is Francis’s cry of hope to cling to Christ through his transitus into the eighth day.

The one who has sung these eight praises—who has let praise become his school of hope in Christ at the hour of death—can sing of death as a sister, knowing she gives a hand to the one passing over from life into new life. While not part of creation, death does become a cause of praise of God.

It is striking that Pope Leo proclaimed the Jubilee of St. Francis just days after the Jubilee of Hope declared by Pope Francis came to its end. It was St. Francis’s hope in Christ, manifested in his sequela Christi at the hour of death and cultivated in his praise of God, that lets us pause and thank God for his holy death—an unarmed and disarming death that witnesses to the peace of Christ.
